intro: Most people never see a big game in person. They hear it on the radio, watch it on a screen, or read the numbers the next morning. Since the 1920s, radio stations, television networks and cable channels have decided which games reach the public and how they look. Those choices shaped what whole cities remember, from the Long Count at Soldier Field in 1927 to the Bulls' last shot in 1998.

Records work in a similar way. A world record or a season total seems like a plain fact. Behind each one stand scorers, governing bodies, rule books and researchers. Equipment, altitude, medicine and rules about who was allowed to compete all affect what a number means. Sometimes a record changes decades later because someone checked the old papers again.

In this unit you will trace sport on radio and television from KDKA in 1920 to ESPN in 1979. You will study how clips and lost tapes shape memory. You will compare records set under different conditions and explain what evidence would make you trust or doubt a mark.
bigQuestion: Who decides what the public sees, hears and counts in sport, and how should we judge the numbers and pictures that reach us?

timeline.t: KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcasts presidential election returns
KDKA carries the first major league baseball game on radio
NBC radio carries the Long Count fight from Soldier Field, Chicago
Hack Wilson of the Cubs sets the single-season RBI record
Joe Louis beats Max Schmeling before a vast radio audience
The first televised major league game airs from Ebbets Field
Congress passes the Sports Broadcasting Act; Roger Maris hits 61 home runs
First Olympic drug tests; Bob Beamon's long jump in Mexico City
ESPN begins broadcasting from Bristol, Connecticut
A redesigned men's javelin starts a new world record list
The World Anti-Doping Agency is founded in Lausanne
MLB recognizes seven Negro Leagues as major leagues

words.d: a program sent out by radio or television for anyone with a receiver
a live report that describes each event of a game as it happens
a group of stations that carry the same program at the same time
a radio broadcast built in a studio from telegraph reports
laws that stop businesses from joining together to limit competition
showing a recorded moment again seconds after it happens on live television
what a whole group of people remembers together about the past
officially approved by a governing body after checking the evidence
the conditions around an event that help explain it
using banned drugs or methods to improve sports performance
facts or records that show whether something is true

test.q: What was special about KDKA's broadcast on August 5, 1921?
choices: It is widely called the first major league game on radio.
It was the first televised game.
It carried the Long Count fight.
It was the first instant replay.
test.why: Harold Arlin called a Pirates and Phillies game from Forbes Field on KDKA.

test.q: Why did New York's baseball clubs keep games off the radio in the 1930s?
choices: Radio was illegal in New York.
They feared free broadcasts would hurt ticket sales.
test.why: Some owners worried free games on the air would empty seats, until the Dodgers broke the agreement in 1939.

test.q: Which Chicago stadium saw Joe Louis win the heavyweight title in 1937?
test.why: Louis beat James J. Braddock at Comiskey Park on June 22, 1937.

test.q: What did the Sports Broadcasting Act of 1961 do?
choices: let leagues sell television rights as one package
test.why: The law exempted pooled league TV deals from antitrust law.

test.q: Who first used instant replay on live American television?
test.why: Verna replayed a touchdown during the Army and Navy game on December 7, 1963.

test.q: Why do many people remember Willie Mays's 1954 catch but not how that game ended?
choices: The catch has been replayed for decades while the rest of the game has not.
Mays won the game with a home run.
The game was on radio only.
test.why: Film of The Catch is shown again and again, shaping collective memory of the game.

test.q: Why was the complete broadcast of Game 7 of the 1960 World Series missing for decades?
choices: The game was never on television.
Many early broadcasts were not saved; one film turned up in Bing Crosby's cellar.
test.why: Networks rarely kept early broadcasts; a full kinescope was found in Crosby's home in 2009.

test.q: Why did Hack Wilson's RBI total change from 190 to 191?
choices: A new scoring rule was passed in 1999.
He hit a home run in 1931.
Research found one RBI had been credited to a teammate.
test.why: Major League Baseball accepted the research and changed the total in 1999.

test.q: What was the main issue in the 1961 argument over Roger Maris's 61 home runs?
choices: The season was 162 games instead of 154.
The games were at high altitude.
test.why: Ford Frick said a record set after 154 games should be shown differently.

test.q: Why did track and field start a new men's javelin record list in 1986?
choices: The Olympics moved to Mexico City.
test.why: Moving the javelin's center of gravity forward made it a different tool.

test.q: What do the 2010 swimsuit rules and the 1986 javelin redesign have in common?
choices: Both came from the Negro Leagues.
Both changed equipment rules because gear was affecting records.
test.why: In each case a governing body changed equipment rules when gear changed what marks meant.

test.q: Which fact about Mexico City in 1968 matters for records?
choices: It is about 2,240 meters above sea level.
test.why: Thin air at high altitude helps sprints and jumps, like Beamon's 8.90 meters.

test.q: Which event pushed sports leaders to found WADA in 1999?
choices: the 1998 Tour de France drug scandal
test.why: Police found banned drugs at the 1998 Tour, and WADA formed the next year.

test.q: Why did many women's distance records begin late?
choices: Women were barred from longer races for decades.
test.why: Women's Olympic races over 200 meters were dropped from 1928 to 1960, and the marathon opened in 1984.

test.q: Which is the best reason to doubt a record?
choices: There is specific evidence, such as conflicting gauge readings or documents.
test.why: Fair doubt names a checkable reason, not just a feeling that a mark is too good.

write.prompt: Pick one record or famous moment from this unit, such as Maris's 61, Beamon's 8.90, Wilson's 191 or Jordan's 1998 shot. Argue how it should be remembered. Cite at least two dates, documents or records from the unit, and explain what each one shows.
tips: Name each document or record you use, such as Frick's 1961 ruling or the 2007 Mitchell Report.
Give the date and place for every event you cite.
Separate what the evidence shows from what people believe or feel.
Explain the context: equipment, altitude, schedule or who was allowed to compete.
Use unit terms such as ratified, revision, context and evidence.
